value.overview: The Slaty-breasted Tinamou is a secretive, ground-dwelling bird of humid tropical forests in Middle America. It spends most of its time walking through leaf litter and dense understory rather than flying. Its low, repeated calls are often the best way to detect it. The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America to northern Costa Rica, where it is a local resident of suitable lowland and foothill forest.
value.classification: The Slaty-breasted Tinamou belongs to the tinamou family, Tinamidae, in the order Tinamiformes. Its scientific name is Crypturellus boucardi.
value.identification: This medium-sized tinamou is about 28 cm long and has a stocky body, short tail, and reddish legs. Adults are generally dark brown above, with black barring on the back and flanks, a gray to slaty-gray head, neck, and upper breast, and warmer buff or rufous lower underparts. The throat is pale. Females may show more extensive buff barring on the upperparts. It is usually seen briefly on the forest floor or detected by its distinctive low call.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a locally resident bird, most associated with the northern Caribbean lowlands and extending south toward Limón. It can occur in foothills to about 700 m and may reach the Pacific slope through mountain passes in the Guanacaste region. Preferred habitat is humid primary or mature secondary forest with dense understory, leaf litter, and moist ground, although it may tolerate some disturbed forest and regenerating plantations.
value.migrationStatus: Slaty-breasted Tinamous are considered resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica, the species remains year-round in suitable forest, including parts of the Caribbean lowlands and nearby foothills; seasonal movements are not known to be significant.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but the species nests on the forest floor in a shallow depression lined with leaves, often among low dense vegetation or near roots. The eggs are typically glossy lavender or purplish. A nest may contain about two eggs, with larger clutches possibly resulting when more than one female lays in the same nest. Males incubate the eggs and care for the chicks. In Costa Rica, nesting has been reported mainly from May through June, possibly continuing into October.
value.dietFeeding: The Slaty-breasted Tinamou forages by walking slowly and irregularly through the leaf litter. Its diet includes fallen fruits, seeds, ants, termites, and other small invertebrates. It may also take small frogs or lizards. Rather than scratching vigorously like domestic poultry, it uses its bill to toss aside leaves and small twigs while searching for food on the forest floor.
value.behavior: This tinamou is mainly solitary and terrestrial. It is most active on the ground and usually relies on camouflage and dense cover. Males defend small territories with repeated calls and may confront rivals. Calling is especially common in the morning and evening, and courtship can involve vocal exchanges between males and females. When alarmed, the bird may freeze or walk away quietly; if closely threatened, it runs through cover and makes a short, noisy flight only as a last resort.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing. Abundance varies locally: the species may remain common in well-protected forest but become scarce where forest is heavily cleared or hunting is intensive.
conservation.threats: Major threats include conversion and degradation of humid forest for agriculture, plantations, pasture, and infrastructure. Fragmentation reduces suitable understory habitat, while hunting can cause local declines because the species is a terrestrial game bird. Continued loss of mature and regenerating forest in Central America is an additional concern.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid lowland and foothill forest, especially in the Caribbean region of Costa Rica. Support protected areas, forest corridors, and shade-grown or wildlife-friendly farming that retains dense native vegetation. Avoid hunting tinamous and discourage the purchase or consumption of wild-caught game birds. Birdwatchers can contribute well-documented sightings to conservation databases and follow quiet, low-impact practices in forest habitat.
